Text hiding behind an empty element

A synthetic probe for the one shape that loses text silently under favor_precision: an empty element whose tail carries the words. Each section below is a producer that really emits one, followed by the near misses that must come through untouched.

The shapes that must survive

A syntax highlighter opens its block with an empty span before the first token, which makes the entire listing that span's tail rather than the block's own text:

def resolve(name):
    target = registry[name]
    return target(**options)

An editor leaves an empty span behind when its author deletes the styled run inside it, and every word after it in the paragraph is that span's tail, which is why a sentence can lose its second half while its first half reads perfectly well aloud.

The same hole opens under a formatting element rather than a span, so an emphasis whose contents were removed swallows the rest of the sentence exactly as an empty span does, and a listener hears the paragraph stop halfway through with nothing marking the loss.

A bold marker emptied by a copy and paste behaves no differently, and this sentence is here to be long enough that its disappearance would be unmistakable rather than something a word count might round away.

A block element left empty by a template that rendered nothing into it sits between paragraphs, and the paragraph after it has to arrive intact.

A wrapper holding nothing but an icon carries no text of its own, so the sentence after it is that wrapper's tail the moment the image is stripped, which is the shape the extractor's own cleaning creates rather than one the page was serving.

The near misses that must not move

An element that holds text is not empty, so this styled run and the words after it are both left exactly where the author put them, and the same is true of a real emphasis and of a real bold run carrying their own content.

An element holding only whitespace has a text node inside it, so it is not empty either: this sentence is the tail of one, and it has to reach the listener whole because trafilatura would not have cut it either.

The same highlighter wrapping its listing in a code element leaves that empty opening span with nothing behind it, so cutting the span costs the block nothing and this is the shape most of the corpus actually uses:

$ nagara enqueue https://example.test/article
queued: 7f3a1c

A closing paragraph, long enough to be a unit of its own, so the block above is bounded on both sides and any leakage past its fences would show up here rather than at the end of the document.
